issues.legal_issue: The governing land-revenue framework permits the government to dispose of unoccupied government land by means other than public auction, including for public-welfare purposes.
material_facts: The government adopted a policy to end public auctions of riverbed cultivation land and allocate leases according to priorities that included bona fide small agriculturists, members of disadvantaged communities, and certain cooperative farming societies.

The applicable land-revenue framework empowered the Collector to dispose of government land and allowed unoccupied land to be granted for cultivation at a fixed price, without charge, or by public auction.
The framework contained no prohibition on disposing of occupancy or leasehold rights by a method other than public auction.
issues.conclusion: The policy was not contrary to the governing framework, and the finding that it was an unauthorized use of statutory power was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on sections 37 and 62, the proviso to section 68, and rules 37, 41, and 42 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code and Rules. Those provisions showed that disposal was not limited to public auction. The Court also considered the framework’s broader public-welfare purpose and the State’s responsibility to distribute resources for the common good under the Directive Principles in Articles 38, 39, and 46. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.appeal_challenges_nonauction_land_dispos: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a ruling that invalidated a government policy for disposing of unoccupied land without public auction.
predicates.government_controls_unoccupied_land: The land at issue is unoccupied land belonging to the government.
predicates.governing_framework_permits_discretionar: The applicable framework allows the authority to dispose of such land through discretionary methods, rather than requiring public auction alone.
predicates.allocation_serves_public_welfare: The allocation policy directs land toward people or groups in need of it for cultivation and livelihood.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges non-auction disposal of government land, the land is government-controlled and unoccupied, the governing framework permits discretionary disposal, and the allocation serves public welfare, the disposal is authorized.

issues.legal_issue: A land-allocation policy that prioritizes disadvantaged and economically weaker cultivators does not violate equality when its classifications reasonably advance equitable access to land.
material_facts: The policy prioritized village agriculturists holding small amounts of land, with preference for members of disadvantaged communities, and also included adjoining small landholders and specified cooperative farming societies.

The policy was intended to help landless people and people with small holdings obtain cultivation land at reasonable rent without having to compete in auctions that had been accessible mainly to people with greater financial resources.
The leases were for limited terms, and the petitioners did not establish that the extent of land covered by the policy made the classification discriminatory.
issues.conclusion: The classification was not arbitrary and did not violate Article 14; the High Court’s contrary finding was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 14, a classification must rest on an intelligible differentia and bear a reasonable relation to the policy’s objective. The Court found that prioritizing landless and small cultivators, disadvantaged communities, and cooperative societies reasonably advanced equitable distribution and social and economic justice. It also relied on Articles 38, 39, and 46. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_allocat: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a policy setting eligibility priorities for allocation of land.
predicates.policy_prioritizes_economically_weaker_c: The policy gives priority to landless or small cultivators, disadvantaged groups, or qualifying cooperative societies.
predicates.auction_access_favors_wealthier_bidders: The circumstances show that public auctions make access to the land substantially harder for economically weaker applicants than for wealthier bidders.
predicates.classification_advances_equitable_land_d: The eligibility categories are reasonably connected to distributing land more equitably and supporting cultivation and livelihood.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a land-allocation policy that prioritizes economically weaker cultivators, auctions favor wealthier bidders, and the classifications advance equitable distribution, the classification is non-arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: A direction protecting claimants from dispossession cannot stand when the court has made no firm finding that they possess the land.
material_facts: The claimants alleged that some of them remained in possession under expired short-term leases, while the government denied that any claimant was in possession when the petitions were filed.
The High Court did not make a firm finding about whether any claimant possessed any part of the land but directed that they not be dispossessed except in due course of law.
issues.conclusion: The direction against dispossession was unsustainable and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the protective direction could not be sustained without a firm factual finding on possession. Although claimants referred to sections 79-A and 202 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, the Court did not decide the substantive application of those provisions. No earlier cases were relied on.

predicates.appeal_challenges_writ_protection_agains: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a writ-court direction protecting claimants from dispossession.
predicates.possession_is_disputed: The claimants assert possession of the land and the government denies that they possess it.
predicates.no_firm_finding_on_possession: The court issuing the protection makes no firm finding that the claimants possess the land.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a writ direction against dispossession, possession is disputed, and the issuing court made no firm finding on possession, the protective direction is unsustainable.
